"title": "Search for High-Energy Gamma-Ray Emission from Anomalous X-ray Pulsar, 4U 0142+61",
"authors": "Sinem Şaşmaz Mus˘ and Ersin Gö˘g˘us˘",
"field_subfield": "High-energy astrophysics / gamma-ray astronomy",
"type_of_paper": "Observational study with spectral and timing analysis",
"executive_summary": "Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) are young isolated magnetars whose hard X-ray and soft gamma-ray emission has long challenged theoretical models. Until 2004 these objects were known only as soft X-ray emitters below 10 keV, but the discovery of a hard X-ray component from several AXPs provided crucial insight while leaving the emission origin unresolved. This paper investigates the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61, using the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to establish the spectral behavior over a very broad energy span and to search for pulsed emission. The LAT operates in the 20 MeV–300 GeV band, providing unprecedented data quality for these sources. The authors accumulated LAT data within a 15° radius centered on 4U 0142+61, collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29 with an exposure of approximately 31.7 Ms, and performed spectral analysis using a 2° radius region to avoid contamination from nearby bright sources. They employed contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations to obtain the spin ephemeris of the source. The results show that 4U 0142+61 is clearly not detected in the LAT energy passband, yielding no significant detection for either persistent or pulsed high-energy gamma-ray emission. The 3σ flux upper limits with a power law index of 2.5 are 2.32 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the 0.2–1.0 GeV band and 1.28 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the 1.0–10.0 GeV band. For pulsed emission, a 3σ upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction is 1.5% in the 0.2–1.0 GeV band, 2.3% in the 1.0–10.0 GeV band, and 1.6% in the lower energy part of the LAT passband (30–200 MeV). These upper limits are much lower than the high pulsed fraction (up to 100%) seen in hard X-rays with INTEGRAL. By constructing the νFν spectrum from 15 keV to 10 GeV, the authors place an upper limit to the spectral break energy at approximately 1.1 MeV, consistent with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007) and the quantum electrodynamics model by Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b). The paper's main contribution is establishing these upper limits to constrain existing physical models. The strongest evidence is the non-detection with robust spectral parameters consistent with catalog values. The future path involves refining these constraints as more data become available and as the origin of the excess optical emission is clarified.",

summary.title: Search for High-Energy Gamma-Ray Emission from Anomalous X-ray Pulsar, 4U 0142+61
summary.authors: Sinem Şaşmaz Mus˘ and Ersin Gö˘g˘us˘
summary.type_of_paper: Observational study with spectral and timing analysis
summary.executive_summary: Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) are young isolated magnetars whose hard X-ray and soft gamma-ray emission has long challenged theoretical models. Until 2004 these objects were known only as soft X-ray emitters below 10 keV, but the discovery of a hard X-ray component from several AXPs provided crucial insight while leaving the emission origin unresolved. This paper investigates the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61, using the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to establish the spectral behavior over a very broad energy span and to search for pulsed emission. The LAT operates in the 20 MeV–300 GeV band, providing unprecedented data quality for these sources. The authors accumulated LAT data within a 15° radius centered on 4U 0142+61, collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29 with an exposure of approximately 31.7 Ms, and performed spectral analysis using a 2° radius region to avoid contamination from nearby bright sources. They employed contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations to obtain the spin ephemeris of the source. The results show that 4U 0142+61 is clearly not detected in the LAT energy passband, yielding no significant detection for either persistent or pulsed high-energy gamma-ray emission. The 3σ flux upper limits with a power law index of 2.5 are 2.32 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the 0.2–1.0 GeV band and 1.28 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the 1.0–10.0 GeV band. For pulsed emission, a 3σ upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction is 1.5% in the 0.2–1.0 GeV band, 2.3% in the 1.0–10.0 GeV band, and 1.6% in the lower energy part of the LAT passband (30–200 MeV). These upper limits are much lower than the high pulsed fraction (up to 100%) seen in hard X-rays with INTEGRAL. By constructing the νFν spectrum from 15 keV to 10 GeV, the authors place an upper limit to the spectral break energy at approximately 1.1 MeV, consistent with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007) and the quantum electrodynamics model by Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b). The paper's main contribution is establishing these upper limits to constrain existing physical models. The strongest evidence is the non-detection with robust spectral parameters consistent with catalog values. The future path involves refining these constraints as more data become available and as the origin of the excess optical emission is clarified.

Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) are young isolated magnetars whose hard X-ray and soft gamma-ray emission has long challenged theoretical models. Until 2004 these objects were known only as soft X-ray emitters below 10 keV, but the discovery of a hard X-ray component from several AXPs provided crucial insight while leaving the emission origin unresolved. This paper investigates the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61, using the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to establish the spectral behavior over a very broad energy span and to search for pulsed emission. The LAT operates in the 20 MeV–300 GeV band, providing unprecedented data quality for these sources. The authors accumulated LAT data within a 15° radius centered on 4U 0142+61, collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29 with an exposure of approximately 31.7 Ms, and performed spectral analysis using a 2° radius region to avoid contamination from nearby bright sources. They employed contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations to obtain the spin ephemeris of the source. The results show that 4U 0142+61 is clearly not detected in the LAT energy passband, yielding no significant detection for either persistent or pulsed high-energy gamma-ray emission. The 3σ flux upper limits with a power law index of 2.5 are 2.32 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the 0.2–1.0 GeV band and 1.28 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the 1.0–10.0 GeV band. For pulsed emission, a 3σ upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction is 1.5% in the 0.2–1.0 GeV band, 2.3% in the 1.0–10.0 GeV band, and 1.6% in the lower energy part of the LAT passband (30–200 MeV). These upper limits are much lower than the high pulsed fraction (up to 100%) seen in hard X-rays with INTEGRAL. By constructing the νFν spectrum from 15 keV to 10 GeV, the authors place an upper limit to the spectral break energy at approximately 1.1 MeV, consistent with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007) and the quantum electrodynamics model by Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b). The paper's main contribution is establishing these upper limits to constrain existing physical models. The strongest evidence is the non-detection with robust spectral parameters consistent with catalog values. The future path involves refining these constraints as more data become available and as the origin of the excess optical emission is clarified.

Methodological Details
The study uses the LAT on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. The LAT operates in the 20 MeV–300 GeV energy band. The LAT is a pair conversion telescope with a silicon tracker. The LAT has been operating as an all sky monitor since 2008 August 4. The LAT data were collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29. The exposure time was approximately 31.7 Ms. The data were accumulated within a 15° radius centered at 4U 0142+61. Spectral analysis used a 2° radius region to avoid contamination. The unbinned likelihood analysis used ScienceTools v9r15p2. The maximum zenith angle was set to 105° to eliminate background. The galactic diffuse emission was modeled with gll iem v02.fit. The extragalactic isotropic diffuse emission used iem v02.txt. The spectral fits were done with the python version of gtlike, pyLikelihood. Photon arrival times were converted to the solar system barycenter. The RXTE PCA is sensitive to photon energies between 2–60 keV. The RXTE HEXTE is sensitive to photons in the 15–250 keV range. Only the PCA observations were employed for the timing analysis. 53 RXTE observations were selected between 2008 August 4 and 2010 April 30. The individual RXTE pointings were typically between 3 and 4 ks long. The total exposure time of all selected observations is about 196 ks. The RXTE/PCA events were extracted in the 2–10 keV range. The arrival times were converted using faxbary tool of HEASoft 6.8.

Procedures And Architectures
The count map image was presented for the 40° radius region. The point source search used the gtfindsrc tool of ScienceTools. The potential source coordinates were inconsistent with 4U 0142+61. The persistent emission fit used a 15° radius region. The fit added all bright cataloged sources and a recently discovered blazar. The persistent emission fit left their model parameters free. The persistent emission fit yielded a Test Statistics value of approximately 0.23. The detection significance was less than 1σ. The 3σ flux upper limits used a power law index of 2.5. The 2° radius region fit used a power law model of index 3. The 2° radius region fit yielded a Test Statistics value of approximately 3. The 2° radius region detection significance was less than 4σ. The pulse profiles were generated in the 0.2–1.0 GeV and 1.0–10.0 GeV ranges. The epoch folding used a Fourier based technique. The pulse profile was generated using three consecutive PCA observations. The observations were grouped to be spaced at least 0.2 days apart. The phase shifts were fit with a 3rd order polynomial. The best fitting model was a 3rd order polynomial with χ²/degrees of freedom = 59.6/42. The spin ephemeris parameters were tabulated in Table 1. The LAT pulse profiles were consistent with random fluctuations. The νFν spectrum was constructed from 15 keV to 10 GeV.
